title: Terrifying moment escaped lion seen stalking the streets of sleepy town
text:
By Adry Torres for Dailymail.com
Published: 18:51 GMT, February 13, 2025 | Updated: 19:10 GMT, February 13, 2025
An escaped lion was seen stalking the streets of a quiet city in Mexico.
The giant beast was captured in video by a passer -by after it was released in San Pedro Cholula, west of Mexico City, Wednesday.
The animal was seen stopping for a moment on a sidewalk while the witness was driving in a vehicle.
The concerned residents alerted the authorities after seeing the Lion wandered through the local roads.
The mayor’s office said in a statement that the incident was investigating.
“The animal was quickly captured and relevant investigations have begun to determine the origin of the incident and avoid future incidents,” said the mayor’s office.
“In the same way, the necessary controls will be carried out to strengthen security measures in the area.”
An image still separated from a surveillance chamber showed a person escorting the lion beyond an open metal door.

Initially, some residents wondered if the lion had escaped an animal sanctuary established in the property once owned by the alleged leader of a gang linked to the Sinaloa cartel.
The property reached the headlines in November 2024 after the police rescued 27 wild animals from the sanctuary, including tigers, lions, panthers and wolves.
At least 40 people were arrested for charges of having ties with the criminal organization.
The incident reminds another in which a 440 pounds of Bengalo wandered through the streets of Tecuala, in the Mexican state of Nayarit, in June 2022.
The Federal Attorney General’s Office for Environmental Protection at the time discovered that the Tigre lacked its claws, but its fangs were intact, and was “good health and without apparent physical injuries.”
A month later, at least 177 lions, tigers, jaguars and other great exotic cats that lived in deplorable conditions in a animal rescue center in Mexico City.
The property of wild animals is legal in Mexico with a permit provided by the office of the Federal Attorney General of Environmental Protection.
